questions.stem: What are tolerance limits in homeostasis?
options: The largest dose of a hormone that a target organ is able to respond to
The fastest rate at which nerve impulses can travel to an effector
The longest time a person can survive without food or water
The upper and lower values of a variable within which cells can function
questions.explanation: Each internal variable, such as temperature or blood glucose, has a range within which the body's cells work properly. Homeostatic mechanisms keep the variable within these tolerance limits.

questions.stem: Body temperature rises during exercise, and sweating continues until temperature falls back towards normal. What kind of control does this show?
options: Positive feedback, because the response is started by a receptor
Negative feedback, because the response begins before any change
Negative feedback, because the response reverses the original change
Positive feedback, because the response increases the original change
questions.explanation: In negative feedback, a change from the normal value triggers a response that reverses it, returning the variable towards normal. Positive feedback would make the change grow larger, as happens with contractions during childbirth.

questions.stem: Why does homeostasis matter to the body's cells?
options: Enzymes and cell processes work well only within narrow conditions
Cells can divide only when the internal environment changes rapidly
Cells need the internal environment to match the external environment
Hormones are produced only when conditions stay exactly at one value
questions.explanation: Cell metabolism depends on enzymes, whose activity is affected by temperature, pH and solute concentrations. Keeping these within limits keeps metabolism running efficiently. The internal environment is kept different from, not matched to, the outside.

questions.stem: Homeostasis involves physiological and behavioural responses. Which is a behavioural response?
options: Shivering when feeling cold
Vasoconstriction in the skin
Increased secretion of thyroxine
Putting on a warm jumper
questions.explanation: A behavioural response is something the person does, such as changing clothing or seeking shade. Shivering, vasoconstriction and hormone secretion are physiological responses that happen automatically.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain acts as the control centre for body temperature?
options: Cerebellum
Medulla oblongata
Corpus callosum
Hypothalamus
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus receives information from thermoreceptors and coordinates responses such as sweating, shivering and changes in skin blood flow.

questions.stem: On a very hot day the air temperature is above body temperature. By which method can the body still lose heat?
options: Conduction to the surrounding air
Convection currents around the body
Evaporation of sweat from the skin
Radiation from the skin to the air
questions.explanation: Radiation, conduction and convection transfer heat from hotter to cooler, so when the surroundings are hotter the body gains heat by these routes. Evaporation of sweat still removes heat, because changing water to vapour uses heat energy from the skin.

questions.stem: When a person becomes hot, the arterioles supplying their skin widen. How does this help lower core temperature?
options: Less blood flows near the surface, so the blood stays cooler in the core
The blood vessels move closer to the surface, so sweat can be produced
The blood vessels release heat-absorbing hormones into the skin cells
More warm blood flows near the skin, so more heat is lost to the air
questions.explanation: When arterioles supplying the skin dilate, more blood flows through skin capillaries, and heat is lost by radiation, conduction and convection. The vessels themselves do not move; they widen.

questions.stem: Which set of responses would the body make when core temperature falls?
options: Sweating, vasoconstriction in the skin and decreased metabolic rate
Shivering, vasoconstriction in the skin and increased metabolic rate
Sweating, vasodilation in the skin and increased metabolic rate
Shivering, vasodilation in the skin and decreased metabolic rate
questions.explanation: When cold, the body reduces heat loss by constricting skin arterioles and increases heat production by shivering and raising metabolic rate. Sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, so they occur when hot.

questions.stem: Which hormones raise the metabolic rate and so increase heat production in cold conditions?
options: Oxytocin and prolactin
Thyroxine and adrenaline
Calcitonin and aldosterone
ADH and aldosterone
questions.explanation: Thyroxine raises metabolic rate over a longer period, and adrenaline (with sympathetic stimulation) raises it quickly. Both increase heat production by cells.

questions.stem: A runner exercising on a hot, humid day overheats more quickly than on a hot, dry day. Why?
options: Humid air causes vasoconstriction, so blood cannot reach the skin surface
Humid air conducts heat into the body much faster than dry air does
Humid air slows sweat evaporation, so less heat leaves the skin
Humid air stops the sweat glands working, so no sweat reaches the skin
questions.explanation: Sweat cools the body only when it evaporates. When the air is already full of water vapour, evaporation slows, so sweat drips off without removing much heat. The sweat glands keep producing sweat.

questions.stem: A bushwalker is caught in cold rain and wind. Her core temperature starts to fall despite shivering. Which explains why wet clothing makes the problem worse?
options: Water in the clothing raises the body's metabolic rate, using up its glucose
Water conducts heat away far faster than air, and evaporation removes more
Wet clothing causes the skin arterioles to dilate, sending more blood to the surface
Wet clothing stops the hypothalamus detecting the change in skin temperature
questions.explanation: Water is a much better conductor of heat than air, and evaporation from wet clothing and skin removes further heat, especially in wind. Behavioural responses, such as changing into dry clothes and seeking shelter, are important here.

questions.stem: Hair erector muscles contract when a person is cold, giving goosebumps. Why does this have little effect on heat loss in humans?
options: Humans have too little body hair to trap a useful layer of insulating air
The muscles contract too slowly to make any difference to heat production
The hairs stand up only in warm conditions, when heat must be lost
The muscles are controlled by hormones, so they respond far too late
questions.explanation: In furry mammals, raised hairs trap a thick layer of still air that insulates the body. Human body hair is too sparse for this, so the response is largely ineffective in humans.

questions.stem: Which cells detect a rise in blood glucose after a meal and respond by secreting insulin?
options: Liver cells that store glycogen
Beta cells of the pancreatic islets
Alpha cells of the pancreatic islets
Cells of the adrenal medulla
questions.explanation: Beta cells in the islets of the pancreas act as both receptor and effector: they detect high blood glucose and secrete insulin. Alpha cells secrete glucagon when blood glucose falls.

questions.stem: Which list gives effects of insulin that lower blood glucose?
options: More glucose uptake by cells, glycogen formation and more glucose use
Breakdown of glycogen in the liver and release of glucose into the blood
Making glucose from amino acids and reducing glucose uptake by muscle
Increased reabsorption of glucose by the kidney and slower use by cells
questions.explanation: Insulin increases the uptake of glucose by muscle and fat cells, stimulates conversion of glucose to glycogen in liver and muscle and to fat, and increases its use in respiration. Breaking down glycogen raises blood glucose and is the action of glucagon.

questions.stem: What is glycogen, and where is most of it stored?
options: A polysaccharide made from glucose, stored mainly in the liver and skeletal muscle
A hormone made from glucose, stored mainly in the pancreas and the adrenal glands
A protein that carries glucose, stored mainly in the blood plasma and lymph
A fat made from excess glucose, stored mainly beneath the skin of the abdomen
questions.explanation: Glycogen is a branched polysaccharide built from glucose units. The liver and skeletal muscles store it. The liver can release glucose from its glycogen into the blood, while muscle uses its own glycogen.

questions.stem: A student skips lunch, and by mid-afternoon her blood glucose is below its normal range. Which response brings it back up?
options: Alpha cells release glucagon, and the liver breaks down glycogen into glucose
Beta cells release insulin, and the liver breaks down glycogen into glucose
Alpha cells release glucagon, and muscle cells take up more glucose from the blood
Beta cells release insulin, and muscle cells convert glucose into glycogen
questions.explanation: Low blood glucose stimulates alpha cells to secrete glucagon, which causes the liver to convert glycogen into glucose and to make new glucose, raising blood levels. Insulin would lower blood glucose further.

questions.stem: How does adrenaline affect blood glucose during a sudden emergency?
options: It lowers blood glucose by increasing the release of insulin from the islets
It raises blood glucose by causing glycogen breakdown in the liver
It lowers blood glucose by moving glucose rapidly into the fat cells
It raises blood glucose by stopping the kidneys from filtering glucose
questions.explanation: Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla quickly stimulates the breakdown of glycogen to glucose, making extra fuel available for muscles in a fight-or-flight situation.

questions.stem: During a long period of stress, cortisol from the adrenal cortex helps keep blood glucose up. How does it do this?
options: It causes the pancreas to release stored glucose directly
It stimulates the liver to make glucose from amino acids
It stimulates the islets to secrete more insulin into the blood
It speeds up the uptake of glucose by most body cells
questions.explanation: Cortisol promotes the formation of new glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, such as amino acids from protein breakdown, and reduces glucose use by many cells. This maintains blood glucose over the longer term, unlike the fast action of adrenaline.

questions.stem: A person with untreated type 1 diabetes has glucose in their urine. Why?
options: Blood glucose is so low that the body excretes glucose to protect the kidney cells
Blood glucose is so high that the kidney tubules cannot reabsorb all the filtered glucose
Without insulin the glomerulus becomes more permeable, so glucose is filtered for the first time
Without insulin the collecting ducts actively secrete glucose from the blood into urine
questions.explanation: Glucose is normally filtered and then entirely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. The carriers that reabsorb it have a maximum rate, so when blood glucose is very high some glucose stays in the filtrate and appears in urine.

questions.stem: In an experiment, a fasting person drinks a glucose solution. Blood glucose rises over 30 minutes, then falls back to normal by 2 hours. Blood insulin rises shortly after glucose rises. What do these results show?
options: Glucagon is released in response to rising glucose and lowers it by negative feedback
Insulin rises in response to glucose and returns it to normal by negative feedback
Insulin is released first and causes glucose to rise, showing a positive feedback loop
Glucose returns to normal without hormones, because cells absorb it at a constant rate
questions.explanation: The rise in insulin follows the rise in glucose, and glucose then falls back to normal, which is negative feedback. Glucagon raises blood glucose, so it would not be released in response to a rise.

questions.stem: Through which routes does the body lose water?
options: Sweat and urine, but never through the lungs
Faeces and exhaled air, but never through sweat
Urine, sweat, faeces and exhaled air
Urine only, because the kidneys control water
questions.explanation: Water is lost in urine, in sweat from the skin, in faeces from the digestive system and as vapour in exhaled air. The kidneys adjust urine output to balance these losses with intake.

questions.stem: Which hormone increases the reabsorption of water from the collecting ducts of the nephron?
options: Growth hormone (GH)
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
Parathyroid hormone (PTH)
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
questions.explanation: ADH makes the distal tubule and collecting duct walls more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood and urine becomes more concentrated. Parathyroid hormone acts on calcium balance, not water.

questions.stem: After several hours without drinking on a hot day, a person's blood becomes more concentrated. Which sequence follows?
options: Chemoreceptors detect it, more aldosterone is released, less sodium is reabsorbed, urine is dilute
The kidneys detect it, more insulin is released, more glucose is reabsorbed, urine is dilute
Osmoreceptors detect it, more ADH is released, more water is reabsorbed, urine is concentrated
Osmoreceptors detect it, less ADH is released, less water is reabsorbed, urine is concentrated
questions.explanation: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise in concentration and the posterior pituitary releases more ADH. The collecting ducts reabsorb more water, so a small volume of concentrated urine is produced and blood concentration falls.

questions.stem: What triggers the thirst reflex, and how does it help water balance?
options: Kidney cells detect dilute urine, and the person drinks to raise urine volume
Osmoreceptors detect concentrated blood, and the person drinks to add water
Chemoreceptors detect low oxygen, and the person drinks to add more oxygen
Thermoreceptors detect high temperature, and the person sweats to lose salt
questions.explanation: When osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a rise in blood solute concentration, they stimulate the thirst centre. Drinking is a behavioural response that adds water and lowers the concentration.

questions.stem: Aldosterone is secreted when blood sodium or blood volume is low. How does it act on the nephron?
options: It increases sodium reabsorption, and water follows by osmosis
It increases sodium excretion in the urine, so blood volume falls
It is released by the posterior pituitary when the blood is dilute
It acts on the glomerulus to increase the rate of filtration
questions.explanation: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex increases sodium reabsorption (and potassium secretion) in the distal tubule and collecting duct. Water follows the sodium by osmosis, so blood volume and pressure rise.

questions.stem: A person loses a large volume of blood. Their blood volume and pressure fall, though the blood's concentration is roughly normal. Which hormone response best restores blood volume?
options: Less aldosterone, so more sodium is lost and water follows
Less ADH, so more water is lost and the urine is diluted
More glucagon, so stored glucose draws water into the blood
More aldosterone, so more sodium and water are reabsorbed
questions.explanation: A fall in blood volume and pressure stimulates aldosterone release. Increased sodium reabsorption draws water back into the blood by osmosis, so volume is restored without changing concentration much. A fall in volume also stimulates ADH release.

questions.stem: Drinking alcohol inhibits the release of ADH. What effect would this have?
options: A small volume of dilute urine, with a fall in blood sodium only
A large volume of dilute urine, with a risk of dehydration
A small volume of concentrated urine, with a risk of fluid overload
A large volume of concentrated urine, with no change in blood volume
questions.explanation: With less ADH, the collecting ducts are less permeable to water, so less water is reabsorbed and a large volume of dilute urine is produced. Fluid loss can leave the person dehydrated.

questions.stem: Which part of the digestive system absorbs most of the water that a person drinks?
options: The oesophagus wall
The small intestine
The large intestine
The stomach wall
questions.explanation: Most water is absorbed in the small intestine, and much of the remainder in the large intestine. Severe diarrhoea reduces water absorption in the intestine and can quickly cause dehydration.

questions.stem: A labourer working in heat sweats heavily for hours and drinks only plain water. Which problem may develop, and why?
options: Low blood glucose, because sweat glands use up the glucose
High blood oxygen, because sweating increases the breathing rate
Low blood sodium, because salt lost in sweat is not replaced
High blood sodium, because plain water contains extra salt
questions.explanation: Sweat contains salts as well as water. Replacing large losses with plain water restores volume but not sodium, so blood sodium can fall. Drinks that contain electrolytes help prevent this.

questions.stem: In the nephron, which section reabsorbs most of the glucose, amino acids, water and salts from the filtrate?
options: The distal convoluted tubule
The proximal tubule
The collecting duct
The glomerulus
questions.explanation: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs all the glucose and amino acids and most of the water and salts. The distal tubule and collecting duct make the final adjustments under the control of ADH and aldosterone.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain contains the respiratory centre that controls the rate of breathing?
options: Pineal gland
Medulla oblongata
Cerebellum
Corpus callosum
questions.explanation: The respiratory centre in the medulla oblongata sends impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, setting the rate and depth of breathing.

questions.stem: Which change in the blood is the main stimulus that increases the rate and depth of breathing?
options: A fall in carbon dioxide, which lowers the blood's pH
A fall in glucose concentration, which raises the blood's pH
A rise in carbon dioxide, which lowers the blood's pH
A rise in oxygen concentration, which raises the blood's pH
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid, so a rise in CO₂ increases hydrogen ion concentration and lowers pH. Chemoreceptors detect this and the medulla increases ventilation. Oxygen has a smaller effect unless it falls a long way.

questions.stem: Where are the chemoreceptors that monitor carbon dioxide and pH for the control of breathing?
options: In the cerebellum and in the walls of the alveoli
In the hypothalamus and in the walls of the bronchioles
In the pituitary gland and in the walls of the trachea
In the medulla and in the carotid and aortic bodies
questions.explanation: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to changes in the hydrogen ion concentration caused by CO₂, and peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies respond to CO₂, pH and low oxygen.

questions.stem: During exercise, how does the autonomic nervous system help supply muscles with more oxygen?
options: Sympathetic nerves slow the heart rate and constrict the bronchioles
Parasympathetic nerves slow the heart rate and constrict the arteries
Sympathetic nerves raise the heart rate and dilate the bronchioles
Parasympathetic nerves raise the heart rate and dilate the bronchioles
questions.explanation: Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate and the force of contraction, raising the delivery of oxygen-carrying blood, and dilates the bronchioles so air flows more easily. The parasympathetic division has the opposite effects at rest.

questions.stem: A swimmer breathes rapidly and deeply for a minute before diving, then holds their breath underwater. Why is this dangerous?
options: It raises oxygen so high that the medulla stops sending any impulses
It lowers oxygen before the dive, so the swimmer starts short of oxygen
It lowers CO₂, delaying the urge to breathe while oxygen keeps falling
It raises CO₂, making the urge to breathe come on far sooner than usual
questions.explanation: The urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising CO₂. Over-breathing removes CO₂, so it takes longer to build up during the dive, but oxygen continues to be used and can fall low enough to cause unconsciousness before the swimmer feels the need to surface.

questions.stem: When a person holds their breath, why do they eventually find it impossible not to breathe?
options: Falling glucose is detected by the pancreas, and adrenaline forces inhalation
Rising CO₂ is detected by chemoreceptors, and the medulla overrides voluntary control
Falling CO₂ is detected by chemoreceptors, and the cerebellum overrides voluntary control
Rising oxygen is detected by osmoreceptors, and the hypothalamus forces exhalation
questions.explanation: As CO₂ accumulates, chemoreceptors send increasing impulses to the respiratory centre in the medulla. Eventually its stimulation of the breathing muscles overrides the conscious effort to hold the breath.

questions.stem: A person travels to a high altitude where the air contains less oxygen. Within minutes their breathing rate increases. Which receptors mainly trigger this response?
options: Thermoreceptors in the skin, detecting the colder air at high altitude
Chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies, detecting low oxygen
Central chemoreceptors in the medulla, detecting a rise in blood oxygen
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, detecting a rise in blood concentration
questions.explanation: The peripheral chemoreceptors are the receptors that respond strongly to a significant fall in blood oxygen. They signal the medulla to increase ventilation. Central chemoreceptors respond mainly to CO₂ and pH, not oxygen.
